kns:
In the old days, when giants still walked the earth, there lived a fisherman and his wife beside the grey waters of the Sound. They had no children, though they had prayed for them all their lives. One morning the fisherman cast his net and drew up a great shimmering egg, bigger than any he had seen. He brought it home, and his wife set it by the fire to warm. That very night the shell cracked open and out tumbled a boy who grew as fast as a birch in summer — by dawn he was the size of a man, and by the next evening he stood taller than the doorframe. They named him Knös, for he was something new under heaven.

As a youth, Knös could lift a boulder that three horses could not budge. He went to the king's court, and the courtiers whispered behind their hands, for never had they seen such a man. The king set him to tasks that defeated all his knights, and Knös performed each one with ease.

Now the king had three daughters, and each had been taken by a fearsome sea troll who dwelt beneath the waves. None of the king's knights could reach the creature's lair, but Knös waded into the grey surf with nothing but his bare hands. Beneath the waves he found the troll's cavern, lit by a sickly green phosphorescence, where the three princesses sat chained to pillars of coral. The troll lunged at him with fangs like broken ship-masts, and the cavern shook with the fury of their battle. Knös seized the creature by its throat and squeezed until the stone walls cracked.

He broke the chains and carried the princesses back to the shore, where the king waited in astonishment. The youngest princess took Knös by the hand and would not let go. At the wedding banquet the goblet from which Knös drank was so heavy that no other man could lift it — and thus it was known that his strength was a gift from the old gods, an echo of Thor himself in the age of men.
lasse-my-thrall:
Once upon a time, in the county of Nerike, there lived a nobleman who had squandered every penny of his fortune. His hall stood empty, his fields gone to seed, and his servants had long since departed.

One night, huddled beneath a bridge to shelter from the rain, he found a scrap of paper wedged between the stones. On it was written a single word: Lasse. The wind whispered that if he spoke the word aloud, something remarkable would happen. He did, and with a clap of thunder there stood before him a man of tremendous frame, with eyes like blue fire.

"What would you have?" asked Lasse. "I am your thrall, and I will do whatever you command." The nobleman ordered a castle built, and by morning it rose from the meadow, its turrets piercing the clouds, its walls hewn from white stone that gleamed like frost. The king declared that whoever could build such a castle should have the princess's hand, and Lasse built a second, finer still, with silver staircases and a roof of beaten gold.

But the nobleman lost the scrap of paper. Without it, Lasse vanished, and the castle crumbled to dust. The nobleman was cast into prison. Yet his young daughter found the paper half-buried in the rubble, spoke the word, and Lasse appeared once more. He rebuilt the castle and freed the nobleman, but this time the lesson was learned: the paper was kept in a locket, and fortune was never taken for granted. For magic may lift a man to the heavens, but only wisdom can keep him there.
finn-the-giant-and-the-minster-of-lund:
In the days when Lund was still a young city, the bishop resolved to raise a minster so great that all of Skane would marvel at it. But no human builder could match the vision, and the work dragged on for years. Then Finn the giant came forward, a creature of immense stature with shoulders broad as a barn door. He offered to finish the minster in a single night, on one condition: the bishop must give him the eyes of Saint Lawrence.

The bishop agreed, though he meant to trick the giant. Finn set to work as the sun dipped below the horizon. He hauled pillars of granite as though they were fenceposts, set arches in place with a single push, and laid tiles faster than a man could count them. The sound of his hammering echoed across the flat plains, and farmers for miles around crossed themselves.

But the bishop had given a secret command: no one in the cathedral was to speak Finn's name. If the giant heard his own name before dawn, the bargain would be broken. The work went well until a nurse in the bishop's household sang a lullaby: "Hush, little one, and sleep, for Finn the giant builds the minster." Her voice carried through the still night, through the open window, and into Finn's great ear.

He froze. A roar of fury shook the vaults, and Finn seized a pillar to tear the roof apart. But the word had been spoken, and the spell was upon him. His feet rooted to the flagstones, his skin greyed and hardened, and his great arms turned to cold and ancient stone. There he stands to this day in the crypt of Lund Cathedral — a giant turned to rock, his fingers clutching a pillar, his face twisted in a snarl of thwarted rage.
the-skalunda-giant:
There was a time when giants lived not in far-off mountains but right here in Sweden, in the great mound of Skalunda that rises from the plains of Vastergotland. The largest of them all was a creature of terrible cunning who had dwelt in the hill since before men built their first villages. But the church bells changed all that. When the villagers cast their first bell and hung it in the new stone church, the sound pierced the hill like a spear of silver. The giant could not bear it. Each peal was a pain that split his skull, and at last he fled Skalunda for good.

He wandered south to the shore, where the sea was grey and restless, and there he found a shipwreck — timbers scattered across the rocks, and three sailors clinging to the hull. He pulled them from the water as easily as lifting driftwood. The sailors trembled, for they did not know what manner of creature had saved them.

The giant drew a great iron bar from the fire he had built on the shore and held it until it glowed white with heat. Then he pressed the bar against the youngest sailor's arm. The blood that welled up was red — unmistakably, undeniably red. "Then you are men," the giant breathed. "I had feared you were something else."

He fed them and warmed them, and when their strength returned, he fashioned a girdle of woven grass and sea-moss, speaking words over it that no mortal tongue could repeat. "Take this to Skalunda, and set it around the oak by the church gate." The sailors carried the girdle home, and that very night the tree began to shake. Its roots tore from the earth, its branches lashed the air, and with a shriek the oak ripped itself free and flew south on a wind that smelled of brimstone. The church bells still ring over Skalunda, but the hill stands empty, waiting for a master who will never return.
yuletide-specters:
It was Christmas Eve, and the snow lay thick on the roads of Uppland. A woman set out on horseback for the midnight mass. She rode hard through the dark forest, the trees cracking with frost, the moon casting blue shadows on the drifts. When she came to the old stone bridge that crossed the frozen creek, she found the way blocked.

Three hags sat on the bridge, hunched like crows on a fencepost. Their hair was the color of ash, and their eyes gleamed with a light not of this world. They cackled when they saw her, and one reached out a bony hand to seize the horse's bridle. The woman spurred her horse and leapt the barrier. Something tore at her cloak — a long strip of wool was ripped away, fluttering in the wind.

She rode on to the church, and the bells were just beginning to ring. But what she found froze the blood in her veins. The pews were full, but every soul in them was headless. Row upon row of figures sat motionless, their necks ending in flat, terrible stumps. At the altar the priest stood in white vestments, raising empty hands toward the ceiling.

The woman screamed and ran. She burst from the church and found her horse had vanished. Behind her she heard the shuffling of dozens of feet on the church steps. She fled into the graveyard, tearing her cloak to shreds, scattering scraps on every grave she passed. Each scrap drew one of the headless dead down to the grave beside it, pawing at the cloth, forgetting her. By the time she reached the road, her cloak was nothing but rags. She rode home and never spoke of it again — but the villagers say that on Christmas Eve you can still hear those bells ringing for a congregation that has no heads to lift in prayer.
silverwhite-and-lillwacker:
In the days when the sea was wider and more terrible than it is now, two brothers set out from their village on the coast of Sweden. The elder was called Silverwhite, for his hair shone like frost on a winter morning; the younger was Lillwacker, small in stature but fierce in heart. They went to seek their sister, stolen away by a sea troll that lived on an island beyond the horizon — the same troll that had murdered their father.

Their journey took them through forests so dark that the sun never touched the ground. In one such forest they found a wounded fox beneath a thorn bush. Silverwhite bound its wounds, and the fox, when it could speak, said: "I will remember your kindness." They came to a river too wide to swim. A great salmon leapt from the water and said, "Share your bread with me, and I will carry you across." Lillwacker broke the loaf in half and held it out.

At last they came to the sea, and the wounded fox waited. "The troll's island lies beyond the third wave. Take this scale from my tail — it will shine brighter than any gold." They waded into the freezing surf, and the troll's island rose from the water like a broken tooth. Inside a cave of black basalt they found their sister, pale and chained to the wall.

Silverwhite held out the glowing scale, and the troll's greedy gaze fixed upon it. In that moment of distraction, Lillwacker darted forward and struck the chains with a stone axe. The links parted, and the sister was free. They fled to the shore with the troll roaring behind them. The fox appeared, and with a flash of its tail the sea rose in a great wall and crashed upon the island. The brothers and their sister walked home through the foam, for in the old tales the bond between faithful brothers is stronger than iron, and no troll can break it.
stompe-pilt:
In a certain parish in Smaland, the people lived in terror of a giant called Stompe Pilt. He stood taller than the church tower, and when he walked the earth shook so hard that milk spilled from pails a mile away. He stole cattle, smashed fences, and demanded tribute from every farmstead.

But there was a shepherd boy, no bigger than a sapling, with eyes bright as a fox's and a tongue sharper than a weathervane. His name was Pilt, and he laughed when the other boys trembled. "Size is just something to hide behind," he said.

One morning Pilt took his sling and a bag of tricks — a flask of tar, a sack of flour, three iron balls, and a live cock — and went to find the giant. "First I must test your strength," he said. "If you can match me, you may eat me. If not, you must leave this parish forever." The giant agreed.

Pilt set his iron balls on the ground. "Squeeze these to dust." The giant squeezed, but the balls burst with tar and flour, covering him in a sticky black mess. The second test was a race, but Pilt had placed his cock on the hilltop. When the giant lumbered up, the bird flew at his face, flapping and crowing, and the giant stumbled back. The third test was the sling. Pilt loaded an iron ball and let fly. It struck the giant square on the forehead. The giant sat down, dazed, and Pilt said, "Will you leave, or shall I try again?" Stompe Pilt lumbered away and never returned. A sharp mind will always best a thick fist, and the smallest person in the room may be the most dangerous of all.
the-girl-and-the-snake:
A girl once wandered deep into the forests of Sodermanland, gathering berries and wildflowers, until the path behind her vanished and the trees closed in on every side. She was lost. The sky was the color of iron, and a cold wind moved through the pines like the breathing of something enormous.

As dusk fell, she came to a clearing where a great snake lay coiled upon a bed of moss. It was as long as a ship's mast, and its scales shimmered with a deep, pulsing green light, like the depths of a lake in summer. The girl should have been terrified, but she was so weary that she simply sank down and wept.

The snake raised its head and spoke, its voice soft and strange, like the rustle of leaves in a warm wind. "Why do you cry, little one?" She told it she was lost. "I will guide you home if you will promise me one thing." "What thing?" "Promise that you will come back to this clearing, and that you will love me."

The girl was desperate and made the promise. The snake led her through the forest with sure and winding grace, and by moonlight she was home. But the promise hung upon her like a chain. Every day she thought of the snake, and every night she dreamed of its green-lit eyes. At last she returned to the clearing.

The snake was waiting. A strange light surrounded them both, and the snake was transformed — not into a prince, but into something between a man and a creature of the forest: beautiful, wild, and ancient. He took her hand, and together they descended into the earth, through tunnels of root and stone, to a hall lit by rivers of gold. The people of Sodermanland say that on a summer evening you can hear singing from beneath the forest floor — the girl and her snake, still keeping their ancient promise.
faithful-and-unfaithful:
Two brothers set out from their father's farm to seek their fortune. The faithful brother carried nothing but a loaf of bread and a kind word for every stranger. The unfaithful brother loaded himself with provisions and a purse of silver, whispering that he would return rich or not at all.

They parted at a crossroads. Along the way, the faithful brother met an old man bent beneath a bundle of sticks and carried it for miles without complaint. The old man revealed himself as a powerful lord and gave the faithful brother a horse, gold, and a letter of introduction to the king. The unfaithful brother, meanwhile, cheated every innkeeper and stole from a merchant who had shown him kindness.

The faithful brother came to the king's court. The king declared that whoever could bring him a pearl from the deepest lake should have the princess's hand. The faithful brother found the lake's spirit trapped by a spell, freed her with a kind word, and received three pearls more brilliant than any the world had seen.

The unfaithful brother stole one of these pearls while his brother slept and presented it to the king. But the faithful brother did not accuse him. "If my brother claims the pearl, let him have the bride. I wish him well." The king, seeing the difference between the two, gave the faithful brother half his kingdom. The unfaithful brother wandered the roads until he died alone. Kindness is a seed that grows into a tree, while greed is a wind that leaves nothing standing.
starkad-and-bale:
There was a hero called Starkad, and there was a trickster called Bale, and between them they were the most feared pair in all the North. Starkad had been raised by Odin himself in the halls of Asgard, trained in the arts of war until no blade could touch him. He had the strength of eight men. Bale was small and cunning, with a tongue that could charm a serpent.

They came together to serve a treacherous king who set them impossible tasks. First he sent Starkad to fell a forest of iron trees that no axe could cut. Starkad bent the trees with his bare hands and piled them like firewood. The king set another task: catch the wild boar that haunted the northern moors, a beast with tusks like scythes. Bale devised the plan — they dug a pit, covered it with branches, and drove the boar toward it. The beast plunged in, and Starkad dispatched it with a single blow.

The final task was the cruelest. The king sent Starkad to the underworld to bring back a goblet of water from the River of Souls. No living man had returned from such a journey. But Bale had studied the old songs: follow the crow that flies backward, speak the names of the dead, and never look behind you. Starkad went down into the dark, past gates of bone and fields of ash. He was almost out when he heard the voice of his dead mother calling his name. He nearly turned, but Bale's warning echoed in his mind, and he walked on.

They brought the goblet to the king, and when he raised it to drink, the water turned to fire and consumed him where he sat. Starkad and Bale walked out the door and no one dared stop them. Brute strength may fell a forest, but it takes a cunning mind to fell a king.
the-werewolf:
In the deep forests of Uppland, there lived a prince who was cursed. Each night at the turning of the moon his body twisted and reshaped, and he became a great grey wolf — not a mindless beast, but a creature of terrible awareness, trapped behind eyes that burned with human sorrow. By day he was a man again, pale and haunted, and he fled the court in shame.

He roamed the wilderness for years, sleeping in caves and hollow trees. The villagers spoke of the wolf in the woods — how it never attacked livestock, how it sometimes left bundles of firewood at the doors of the poor, how lost children were always found safe. But no one knew the wolf's secret.

One autumn evening a princess wandered into the forest. She was gathering mushrooms when she heard a low, mournful howl. She turned and saw the wolf at the edge of a clearing, watching her with eyes too intelligent, too sad to belong to any beast. She did not run. Something in those eyes held her fast.

"I know you are not what you seem," she said. The wolf lowered its great head. She knelt and placed her hand upon its brow, and in that moment the curse cracked — not broken, but cracked, like ice on a river in early spring. The wolf shuddered, and for a single heartbeat it was a man again, and he whispered, "Thank you."

Night after night she returned with bread and warm milk, telling him stories of kings and voyages and stars that guided sailors home. Each story peeled away another layer. On the longest night of winter she placed her hand upon the wolf's head and said, "I love you, not despite what you are, but because of it." The fur fell away like a cloak, and beneath it stood a man — young, trembling, and free. The curse was broken not by a sword or a spell, but by a love that saw through the beast to the soul beneath.
first-born-first-wed:
A king and a queen made a pact before their children were born: whichever bore a son and whichever bore a daughter, the two should wed. The queen bore a boy, and the king bore a girl, and the promise was sealed. But the king died, and the queen remarried a man whose heart was cold and calculating.

The new king wanted his own daughter on the throne. He sent the prince on quests from which no man could return, hired assassins, and tried exile. But the prince survived each trial — crossing mountains of ice, navigating seas of strange fire, fighting nameless creatures. At each turning some hidden power guided him: a white bird, a whisper in the wind, a dream that would not let him sleep.

The princess, meanwhile, sat in her tower, tended by a cruel stepmother who dressed her in rags and called her a scullery maid. But the princess was not broken. She tended the garden, and flowers grew where none had grown before. She sang at the well, and the water turned to wine. The servants whispered she had magic in her blood.

At last the prince came to the kingdom. He did not recognize the scullery maid, nor she him, but their hearts knew each other. He showed her the ring his mother had given him, inscribed with the words of the old oath. She showed him the scar on her wrist where the same oath had been branded in fire. They embraced, and the spell shattered.

The wicked queen tried to flee, but the ground opened and swallowed her. The prince and princess were married with a feast that lasted seven days. The promise sealed at birth was sealed by fate, and no human cunning could unmake it.
the-mount-of-the-golden-queen:
There was a poor boy in Sodermanland who tended cattle on the hillsides and slept in a hut of sticks and moss. He had no father and no mother, but he had a kindness that could not be mocked — he fed sparrows from his own bread, spoke gently to the oxen, and never passed a wounded creature without stopping.

One evening he saw an old woman struggling with a heavy bundle on the forest path. He took it without being asked and carried it for miles. When they reached a great mound covered in wildflowers, the old woman smiled: "Remember this place, and return when the moon is full."

He returned on the appointed night, and the mound had opened. Inside was a hall of carved wood and amber, lit by candles that burned without smoke. At the far end sat a queen of gold, radiant as the sun, her crown studded with jewels that shifted like northern lights. She was the queen of the hidden folk.

"Your kindness has opened the door. Ask for whatever you wish." He asked for nothing for himself — only that his cattle might be healthy, his neighbors prosperous, and the birds always fed. The golden queen smiled and gave him a pouch of gold and a cloak that made the wearer invisible to thieves and wolves. But the real gift was a blessing: nothing he planted would fail, and nothing he would touch would break.

He traveled the world, leaving kindness behind him. At last he returned to Sodermanland, and the golden queen appeared once more: "You have done well. Now take my hand and live in the mountain forever." The farmers of Sodermanland still leave a bowl of milk on the hilltop at midsummer, and if it is gone by morning, they know the golden queen is pleased.
old-hopgiant:
Old Hopgiant was not like other giants. He was shorter than most, with a beard like grey lichen and eyes that twinkled with a light that had nothing to do with magic — or perhaps everything to do with it. He lived in a hut at the edge of the forest, and the villagers avoided him, saying he was a troll and trolls were not to be trusted.

But there was a poor peasant — the poorest in the parish — who had nothing left but a single cow, a sack of barley, and a wife who coughed in the winter. One night, when the wind howled and the snow piled against the door, there came a knock. The peasant opened it, and there stood Old Hopgiant, shivering, his cloak torn, his feet bare in the frozen mud.

"May I come in? I am hungry, and the cold is deep." His wife tugged at his sleeve. "He is a giant. He will eat us." But the peasant said, "He is cold and hungry, and that is enough." He set the giant by the fire and shared his barley broth.

Old Hopgiant ate until the pot was empty, then smiled a slow, wide smile. "I have no silver to repay you, but I have this." He produced a small wooden mill. "Set it on the table and say 'Grind, little mill, grind,' and it will produce whatever you ask. But when you have enough, say 'Stop,' or it will grind until the house is buried."

The peasant said, "Grind, little mill, grind." Flour poured forth like snow. "Stop, little mill, stop!" The mill fell silent. A greedy neighbor stole the mill and commanded gold to grind, but when he tried to say stop, the words tangled in his throat. Gold filled the room and buried the house. The peasant retrieved the mill, and the tale was told for generations: the best magic is the kind you use with care.
the-princess-and-the-glass-mountain:
At the edge of the world, where the forests gave way to frozen tundra, there stood a mountain made entirely of glass. It rose from the plain like a spear thrust into the belly of the sky, its surface smooth and treacherous. At the summit sat a princess, and the king her father declared that whoever could ride to the top should have her hand.

Knights came from every kingdom. They spurred their warhorses at the base and were thrown before they had climbed ten paces. The glass was too smooth, too steep, and the wind that circled the peak was a living thing, shrieking and clawing at anything that dared ascend.

Then came a poor boy — no armor, no crest, no entourage. He had nothing but a horse with a coat like polished ebony and eyes that held a strange, knowing light. The horse set its hooves upon the glass and did not slip. It climbed steady as a heartbeat, and the wind parted before it like a curtain.

The princess watched from the summit. The boy reached the top and dismounted, young, with wind-burned skin and hands rough from labor. "Will you have me?" he asked. "I have nothing to offer but myself." The princess descended the mountain behind him, and the kingdom watched in astonishment.

The king was furious, but the princess spoke: "You promised the mountain to whoever could climb it. Your oath is sworn." They were married, and the glass mountain melted in the spring rains and became a lake, clear as the sky. For the mountain was never the obstacle — the obstacle was the pride of men who believed worth could be measured in gold and steel.
queen-crane:
In a kingdom far to the north, there lived a poor shepherd boy named Proud. He was called Proud not because he was vain, but because he would not bow to anyone, not even the king. He tended his sheep on the hillside and sang to them in a voice so sweet that the birds themselves fell silent.

One day a great crane flew down and landed beside him. Its feathers were white as snow, its legs long and red as coral. It spoke in a voice like a bell: "I am a queen, enchanted by a sorcerer who was jealous of my beauty. If you will serve me faithfully for three years, I shall be free."

Proud agreed. For three years he built the crane a nest of the finest reeds, fetched her fish from the river, and shielded her from winter winds with his own cloak. The other shepherds mocked him, but Proud kept his word.

At the end of three years the crane shed its feathers and stood before him as a woman — tall, golden-haired, with eyes the color of a glacier at midday. "To break the spell completely, I must undergo three transformations, and you must not be afraid." She turned first into a great fire that consumed the hillside. Proud stood firm. She turned into a roaring river. Proud stood firm. She turned into a storm of black wind. Proud stood firm.

When the storm passed, the queen stood before him, whole and radiant, the spell broken. She took his hand and led him to the kingdom, where the sorcerer had long since fled. They were crowned together, and Proud bowed to her, and she to him. Faithfulness is its own reward, but sometimes the reward is a queen.
tales-of-the-trolls:
There are three tales of trolls, and each carries a warning.

The first is of a peasant who found a spring in the forest and knelt to drink. A voice behind him said, "That is my spring." He turned and saw a troll — grey-skinned, with a nose like a turnip and eyes like burning coals. "Your spring? There is water enough for both of us." The troll considered this and nodded. They drank together, and the troll told him where to find a treasure beneath an old birch tree.

The second tale is of a girl who met a handsome young man by the road on her way to a dance. He wore fine clothes and smiled like summer. "Come with me, and I will show you a palace beyond your dreams." She took his hand and they walked into the mountain. Inside was a hall lit by thousands of candles, and trolls in silks danced to music beautiful and strange. When morning came she found herself in a field, her clothes torn, her hair filled with moss and dead leaves. She had been taken by the mountain — what the old people called bergtagning.

The third tale is of a farmer who woke to find his grain store empty. He set a trap — a great iron pot filled with boiling porridge by the door. That night the troll reached for the pot and plunged its arm to the shoulder in the scalding gruel. It howled and fled, leaving a trail of porridge and blood. The farmer followed the trail to the troll's lair and found his grain — and more besides. These three tales remind us that trolls are not always dangerous, but they are always hungry.
the-three-dogs:
In the kingdom of Vastergotland, there lived a king who had everything — a queen who loved him, a castle of white stone, and fields that yielded tenfold. But an evil witch-queen in a tower of black granite cast a spell older than the hills: the king fell into a sleep so deep that when he opened his eyes, he did not know his wife, his children, or his kingdom.

The queen knew that only three enchanted dogs could break the spell. She set out across three kingdoms and over seven mountains. In the first she found a dog the size of a pony, with a bark that shook the earth — the Dog of Strength. In the second, a dog that ran faster than the wind — the Dog of Speed. In the third, a dog that sang a low, haunting melody that could make stone weep — the Dog of Music.

She brought them home, and that night she led them into the throne room. The Dog of Strength barked, and the windows rattled. The Dog of Speed ran circles around the throne until a whirlwind spun in the air. And the Dog of Music sat at the king's feet and sang — a song so beautiful, so full of sorrow and love, that it cut through the spell like a blade through silk.

The king opened his eyes. He saw his wife. He saw his children. He wept. The witch-queen's tower crumbled to dust that very night, for the spell was broken and the magic returned to the earth. On quiet nights in Vastergotland you can still hear the Dog of Music singing — a reminder that in the war against darkness, the most powerful weapon is not a sword but a melody.
the-poor-devil:
One day a poor peasant from Smaland knelt in his field and prayed — not for riches, but for the safety of his cow. "Dear God, if anything should happen to Bessie, I would have nothing left." A voice from above replied: "Your cow is in My hands." But from the shadows another voice cut in: "In your hands? She is in my hands! I can take her whenever I please." It was the Devil, stepping out from behind a haystack with a smirk.

God said: "Very well. Let us make a wager. You claim you control the fate of this peasant's cow. If you can take her without his consent, you win. If you cannot, I win."

The Devil set to work. He sent a wolf to the pasture, but the dog chased it away. He sent a storm to flatten the barn, but the peasant rebuilt it before nightfall. He sent sickness, and the peasant's daughter nursed the cow with herbs and songs. He sent a flood, and the cow climbed to high ground. He sent fire, and the cow walked calmly through the smoke.

At last the Devil sat down, panting and furious. "The creature is bewitched." God smiled: "She is not bewitched. She is loved. That is something you have never understood, and never will." The Devil conceded and slunk back to his realm, muttering. The peasant's cow lived to a ripe old age, and the field where she grazed was the greenest in all of Smaland. The Devil may be powerful, but he cannot compete with a good heart and a steady hand.
how-smaland-and-schonen-came-to-be:
In the beginning, when God was making the world, the Devil watched with envy. "I can do what you do. Give me a handful of earth and I will make a land of my own." God, who is patient with fools, gave him a handful.

The Devil took the earth and tried to shape it into a plain — flat and fertile, with soil so rich that anything would grow. But just as he finished, a frog leapt from the bushes and landed in the middle of his plain, leaving a deep, ugly mark. The Devil cursed and tried to smooth it out, but the damage was done. That is why Smaland is full of rocks and holes — the Devil's first attempt, ruined by a frog.

He tried again. This time he shaped the earth into rolling hills, green and gentle, with streams in the valleys. But God looked at the work and sent a great flood that covered the land and washed away the Devil's careful shaping. When the waters receded, all that remained was a flat, featureless plain of the richest soil in all the North.

The Devil stared in fury, for he had wanted mountains and dramatic scenery, and instead he had made a pancake. That is Skane — flat as a millstone, fertile as paradise, and entirely by accident. The Devil abandoned it in disgust, and the people of Skane were well content with their fine farmland. The people of Smaland cleared the stones and planted their crops and said, "If the Devil made our land, then we have beaten him at his own game."
the-evil-one-and-kitta-grau:
Kitta Grau was a woman of Halland — old, sharp-tongued, and not the sort to be trifled with. She had outlived two husbands, raised seven children, and argued with every tax collector, priest, and landlord in the county. She feared nothing on earth.

One evening the Devil came to her door in his best coat and polished boots. "Good evening. I have come for your soul." Kitta looked him up and down. "My soul is not for sale, and you are standing on my clean doorstep. Wipe your feet."

The Devil was taken aback. He offered her gold; she demanded double. He offered youth; she demanded triple, plus new teeth. He offered power over neighbors; she said she already had that. At every turn she out-bargained him.

At last he said, "What do you want? Name your price." Kitta leaned back and smiled. "I want you to leave Halland and never come back. And take this terrible coffee with you." The Devil gathered his coat and his dignity and left. He did not return.

Kitta Grau lived to ninety-seven, and when she died the Devil sent a card. It read: "Congratulations." There is no power on earth — or beneath it — that can match the wit of a woman who refuses to be afraid.
the-lady-of-pintorp:
In the old days, Pintorp Castle stood on a hill overlooking the forests of Ostergotland, its walls of grey stone rising from a mist that never quite lifted. The lady who lived there was known throughout the county for her cruelty. She beat her servants, starved her tenants, and laughed at the poor who begged at her gate. The priests said she had made a pact with the Devil.

She died as she had lived — in rage, screaming curses at the servants who attended her final moments. They buried her in the chapel, and the castle was silent for a time. But silence, in Pintorp, was only the prelude.

On stormy nights, when the wind howled from the east, the villagers heard it — a carriage racing along the road, wheels on wet stone, horses' hooves striking sparks. They saw it: a great black carriage, drawn by four black horses, their manes streaming like banners of smoke. It raced up the hill, circled the courtyard three times, and vanished through the gates.

Those brave enough to follow found the courtyard empty. But the chapel doors were open, and the stone coffin of the lady was cracked, and a cold wind blew from within, carrying the smell of sulfur and old roses. The priest who tried to seal it with holy water found the water turn to blood.

For generations the ghost haunted castle and road alike. When the castle fell to ruin, the haunting ceased — or so they said. But on stormy nights the old men still cross themselves and whisper, "The Lady rides tonight." Cruelty does not die with the body. It lingers, and it rides, and it waits for a door left open in the dark.
the-specter-in-fjelkinge:
In the village of Fjelkinge, in the province of Skane, there lived a man known for his honesty. He was a farmer, plain and hardworking, with a wife and three children and not an enemy in the world. But envy grows in dark soil, and a neighbor who coveted his land conspired with a corrupt bailiff to accuse the farmer of theft. The evidence was fabricated, the witnesses bribed, and the farmer was condemned.

He pleaded his innocence at the gallows. "I have not stolen. God knows my heart." The rope tightened, and he was dead.

That night the true murderer could not sleep. The shadows in the corner of his room began to move, and a shape emerged — pale, translucent, with the farmer's face and steady eyes. It did not speak. It simply stood there, watching, its gaze heavy as a millstone. He screamed and lit every candle, but the specter did not leave.

Night after night it came. It followed him to the field, to the church, to the marketplace. Others began to see it too — a pale figure walking the roads in the grey hours before dawn. The guilty man grew thin and wild-eyed. He confessed at last, and the corrupt bailiff was arrested. The farmer's name was cleared.

But the specter did not leave. It walked seven more nights, slower now. On the eighth night it appeared at the farmer's grave, knelt, and pressed its pale hands to the earth. Then it rose, and a light surrounded it — warm, golden, like morning — and it was gone. The ground where it knelt grew green before all the rest, and the grass there is still greener today. Innocent blood calls for atonement, and justice, though slow, is never forgotten.
the-rooster-the-hand-mill-and-the-swarm-:
A poor peasant once traded his last pig for three things no one else wanted: a rooster, a hand-mill, and a hornets' nest. His wife nearly fainted. "You have traded our livelihood for rubbish!" But the peasant said, "Everything has its use, if you know how to use it."

He was right. The rooster laid golden eggs — small, bright, and pure as sunlight. The hand-mill ground out flour, salt, and sugar in any quantity. And the hornets' nest housed a swarm of the fiercest hornets in all the North, each as big as a man's thumb.

A greedy innkeeper heard of these wonders and stole them while the peasant slept. But the peasant was not as drugged as he seemed. He retrieved the hand-mill, then set the hornets' nest on the innkeeper's windowsill and knocked at the door.

The innkeeper opened it with a smug smile, but the peasant wound the mill and said, "Grind, little mill, grind." Flour filled the room. The innkeeper lunged, but the peasant grabbed the rooster and ran. The innkeeper gave chase, and the peasant released the hornets. They poured through the inn like a living storm, stinging every inch of the greedy man's skin. He howled and ran three miles before they returned to their nest.

The peasant walked home with his treasures, and his wife greeted him with tears of joy and a scolding that lasted until supper. Never despise what you do not understand, and never steal from a man who has hornets on his side.
torre-jeppe:
In the church of Torreberga, in the province of Skane, there sat a mummified corpse. It had sat there for as long as anyone could remember — a withered, leathery thing dressed in the clothes of a man who had died a century ago, propped upright in a pew as though waiting for a sermon. The villagers called it Torre Jeppe.

A sexton decided to keep watch. He sat in the church from dusk to dawn, a lantern at his feet and a Bible in his hands. Just before midnight he heard it — a sound like dry leaves scraping across stone.

The corpse was moving. Its head turned toward the sexton. Its mouth opened, and from its throat came a voice like wind through a keyhole: "Do you know why I sit here?" The sexton did not run. "Tell me."

"I was a man of this parish. I wronged my neighbor. I took his land by lies and forged papers, and he died in poverty while I grew rich. When I died, I could not rest. They carried me here, and I have sat ever since, waiting for justice."

The sexton traced the old records, found the descendants, and restored the stolen land. The next morning the pew was empty. Torre Jeppe was gone. In his place lay a pile of dust and neatly folded clothes. The sexton buried the dust in consecrated ground and said a prayer. On quiet nights, the people say, you can hear a sigh of relief from beneath the floor. Wrongdoing does not end with death — the guilty carry their chains into the grave, and only the living can set them free.
